title: Software-only multi-node TDOA/AoA interference and rogue-emitter geolocation engine on commodity SDR nodes, plus an offline-first spectrum-management workflow client (JRFL/SFAF assignments, interference tickets) for installation, range and shared-band spectrum managers
problem: Installation, range and shared-band spectrum managers who receive an interference complaint still locate the source by sending a technician out with a handheld analyzer and then file the ticket by hand into DISA's online JSIR/Spectrum XXI tools, because affordable multi-node geolocation software and an offline-capable ticket/assignment client do not exist below the premium CRFS/Rohde & Schwarz/Keysight price tier.
echelons: test and training range frequency management office
brigade/division 25E spectrum manager (disconnected workflow use only)

user.exact_role: Installation spectrum manager (Army NEC/G6 installation spectrum manager; Air Force base spectrum manager under DAFI 17-221), range frequency manager, and unit 25E spectrum manager filing JSIR interference reports
organization_examples: Army installation Network Enterprise Centers (NETCOM) and Army Spectrum Management Office
Air Force base communications squadrons (spectrum management per DAFI 17-221)
Test and training range frequency management offices (e.g., major Army/AF/Navy ranges - names not verified this session)
DISA Defense Spectrum Organization / Joint Spectrum Center (JSIR process owner)
CBRS SAS administrators and private-5G operators; FCC/NTIA enforcement (civil)

current_workflow: 1. Interference report arrives by phone, email or chat from a unit, tenant or neighbor.
2. Spectrum manager checks assignments in Spectrum XXI (mandated frequency request tool) and local records to see who is authorized on the frequency.
3. If the source is unknown, a technician drives out with a handheld analyzer (or a rented/loaned CRFS/R&S node) and manually direction-finds over hours to days.
4. Manager files or updates a JSIR report in JSIRO (Joint Spectrum Interference Resolution Online) per CJCSM 3320.02E; unresolved cases escalate to the Joint Spectrum Center.
5. For drone/rogue-emitter cases a separate C-UAS or passive-sensing stack (Hidden Level, Dedrone) with its own dashboard is consulted if the installation has one.
6. When disconnected (field CP, range, DDIL), assignments/JRFL and EMI tickets are kept in spreadsheets and re-entered later.
current_solution: Handheld analyzers plus drive-testing; premium fixed monitoring networks (CRFS RFeye with AoA/TDoA/PoA, Rohde & Schwarz hybrid AOA/TDOA systems, Keysight KSMS TDoA with three FieldFox units) where funded; Hidden Level passive-sensing networks now scaling over bases/ranges under a $100M-ceiling OTA; for Army tactical units S2AS (3dB Labs) which explicitly supports EMI resolution and warns of unauthorized interference sources; DISA enterprise tools (Spectrum XXI, JSIRO, JSDR, E2ESS, EMBM-J) for assignments and tickets; hobby/low-cost coherent DF (KrakenSDR with RDF Pro multi-station fusion) and small vendors such as Wavelet Lab offering multi-node SDR TDOA/FDOA platforms; spreadsheets when offline.
failure: It fails at two points: (a) below the premium tier there is no trusted, self-calibrating multi-node geolocation product an installation can afford for whole-base persistent coverage, so most sites do not geolocate at all and rely on drive tests; (b) the assignment/JRFL/JSIR workflow is enterprise-hosted (Spectrum XXI, JSIRO) and is not usable offline at ranges or field CPs, so data is re-keyed. Neither failure has a named requirement owner or budget line for a third-party software product; the funded responses (Hidden Level OTA, S2AS, REWSI sensors, EMBM-J recompete) are hardware-plus-software buys from already-selected vendors or DISA-captive tools.

evidence.claim: DISA DSO sought sources for a SOSC helpdesk providing Tier I/II technical and EMS operational support for Spectrum XXI, JSIRO (Joint Spectrum Interference Resolution Online), JSDR and E2ESS for Sept 2021-Sept 2026, confirming that interference tickets and assignments run on DISA-hosted online tools with a services support contract, not a tactical/offline client.
evidence.source_title: SAM.gov - DSO SOSC Helpdesk sources sought
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: CJCSM 3320.02E defines the Joint Spectrum Interference Resolution process: EMI events are resolved at the lowest level and the Joint Spectrum Center is the center for EMI reporting, analysis and tracking from initial report to resolution; spectrum managers consult the Spectrum XXI database to determine EMI causes. Establishes that the ticket workflow is doctrinal and government-owned.
evidence.label: FACT

Ceiling, not revenue; obligations not public.

The geolocation algorithms are commodity at the premium tier; the gap is price, not capability.

why_existing_startups_havent_solved: They have, at every price point that has a paying buyer: premium vendors (CRFS, R&S, Keysight) sell hybrid AoA/TDoA systems to regulators, ranges and installations that can afford them; Hidden Level took the persistent base/range passive-sensing buyer under a $100M-ceiling OTA; 3dB Labs (S2AS) and the REWSI vendors (Heaviside, RII) took the Army tactical EMI-detection buyer with sensors bundled with software; Distributed Spectrum ($29M raised, AFRL SBIRs incl. localization algorithms) and Wavelet Lab already sell the low-cost-SDR-plus-software version; KrakenSDR ships RDF Pro. What remains - the sub-premium installation buyer with no sensor budget and the offline ticket client - is unsolved because that buyer has no requirement owner, program office or line (installation spectrum managers are records/compliance staff under NEC or the comm squadron), DISA DSO already owns the ticket workflow in JSIRO/EMBM-J, and the civil side is thin and price-sensitive (Aurora Insight precedent; CBRS interference is resolved by SAS administrators and measurement campaigns are run by NIST/ITS/MITRE).
technical_wedge: A hardware-free engine that turns 4-12 commodity coherent/GPSDO-synced SDR nodes (KrakenSDR/RTL-SDR/USRP class) into a self-calibrating TDOA+AoA geolocation service with honest per-fix CEP, multipath/false-alarm suppression tuned for dense installation RF, automatic matching of detections against an imported SFAF assignment list (authorized vs unauthorized), and a JSIR-format ticket generator; plus an offline-first client (web/WinTAK/ATAK-CIV plugin) that holds assignments, JRFL entries and tickets locally under DDIL and syncs to Spectrum XXI/JSIRO exports when connected. Explicitly excludes threat-emitter identification, EW/ES functions and any military-specific DF hardware to stay on the EAR side (needs counsel).

mvp.what: 6-node KrakenSDR/RTL-SDR+GPSDO network on a university campus or private land, a fusion service producing geolocations with CEP and confidence for cooperative ISM/amateur emitters, an SFAF-import authorized/unauthorized classifier using synthetic assignment data, and an offline JSIR-style ticket queue that syncs to a mock JSIRO export.
mvp.demonstrable_in_3_6_months: Yes: cooperative-emitter CEP curves over 1 km^2, time-to-locate under 30 minutes versus a manual drive test, ticket produced offline and synced after a simulated 60-minute outage.
mvp.what_it_must_prove: That cheap, imperfectly synchronized nodes reach a stated CEP (e.g., tens of meters) with a low false-fix rate in a dense campus RF environment; that a spectrum manager can produce a JSIR-format ticket offline faster than with spreadsheets; and - the hard part - that a named installation or range office will pay for it rather than wait for Hidden Level/S2AS/enterprise tools.

data_requirement.what: Multi-node time-synchronized IQ/detection recordings of installation-typical emitters (LMR, Wi-Fi, LTE/CBRS, ISM, GPS-jammer analogs where legal), site calibration data, SFAF-format assignment records, JRFL entries and JSIR ticket samples.
data_requirement.legally_realistically_obtainable: RF recordings: yes, self-collected on receive-only SDRs at a campus or with cooperative transmitters (FCC rules on content disclosure apply). SFAF/JSIR formats: public references (CJCSM 3320.02E, ATP 6-02.70) allow synthetic data. Real installation assignments, JRFL (may be classified) and JSIR records are CUI or classified and require a government sponsor; export-controlled CUI is effectively U.S.-person-only (E07-F30), so the Indonesian founder cannot handle it.

entry_vehicle.primary: No direct vehicle exists. Realistic paths are (a) a paid civil pilot with a private-5G/CBRS operator, range or airport GPS-interference team, (b) a CRADA with an installation NEC/comm squadron or with DISA DSO/JSC for the offline JSIR client, (c) a subcontract to a sensor OEM (Hidden Level, Heaviside, RII, Distributed Spectrum) or the GEMSIS/EMBM-J contractor as a software feature.
sequence: Build the 6-node campus demo and publish CEP/false-fix results and an open SFAF/JSIR toolkit (0-6 months, founder capital)
Land 2-3 paid civil pilots (CBRS/private-5G operator, test range, event venue) to refute the Aurora Insight precedent
Secure a CRADA or OTA-funded pilot with one installation or DISA JSC for the offline JSIR client, with U.S.-person staff handling CUI
Pitch the geolocation engine as a licensed module to a sensor OEM or the EMBM-J/EWPMT-X integrator
Only if an enterprise owner (IMCOM/AFIMSC/DISA DSO) issues a requirement: compete on a CSO/OTA
entry_vehicle.eligibility_notes: SBIR/STTR require >50% ownership and control by U.S. citizens or permanent residents (13 CFR 121.702; corpus E07-F3): the Indonesian founder's shares never count and the German founder's count only after the green card, so a 50/50 team fails unless the cap table is restructured (counsel). OTA/CSO/CRADA carry no citizenship test, but export-controlled CUI (assignments, JRFL, JSIR records) is effectively U.S.-person-only (E07-F30), so the Indonesian founder must be walled off from government data. Receive-only civil spectrum-monitoring software is plausibly EAR (5A001/5D001 or EAR99) rather than ITAR if it is not specially designed for military EW/DF - a commodity jurisdiction/classification review by counsel is required before design; ITAR treats the German founder as a U.S. person only on permanent residence (22 CFR 120.62).

incumbent_response.could_anduril_palantir_l3harris_add_it: Yes, and mostly they need not bother: R&S/CRFS/Keysight already sell the geolocation capability and can add a low-cost tier; Distributed Spectrum and Hidden Level can license their fusion to run on cheaper nodes; Palantir (EMBM-J DS) and the GEMSIS contractor can add an offline/sync mode to DISA's tools on DISA's request; the EWPMT-X integrator can absorb an offline JRFL/JSIR client as a TAK capability drop; Anduril and L3Harris have no reason to enter a sub-$50k-per-site market.
incumbent_response.why_startup_still_wins_or_reject: Reject as a standalone venture. The only argument for a startup is price and usability at the neglected installation tier, but that tier has no procurement authority and buys handhelds, and the two funded routes into it (Hidden Level's OTA and DISA's tools) are already occupied. A startup could win only as a feature/licensed module inside an OEM or integrator product, or as a small civil SaaS - a consultancy/feature path, not a venture-scale outcome.

regulatory_burden.explanation: Receive-only spectrum monitoring on COTS SDRs is legal domestically (FCC rules limit disclosure of intercepted content); a civil-scoped geolocation/workflow product that is not specially designed for military EW/DF is plausibly EAR (5A001/5D001 or EAR99) rather than USML Category XI, but direction-finding features aimed at military users can drift toward Category XI - only a commodity jurisdiction/classification review settles it. All real assignment, JRFL and JSIR data is CUI (JRFL may be classified), so any government pilot brings DFARS 252.204-7012/NIST SP 800-171/CMMC obligations. No clearance is needed for the civil product; a classified JRFL module would require a cleared facility and U.S.-citizen staff. None of this is a legal judgment.
regulatory_burden.non_us_person_founder_note: If the product stays EAR99/EAR-dual-use the Indonesian founder is largely unconstrained on the engine and client code (E07-F17), but must be excluded from export-controlled CUI supplied by any government sponsor (E07-F30) and cannot count toward SBIR ownership (13 CFR 121.702). The German founder becomes a U.S. person for ITAR only on permanent residence (22 CFR 120.62). A CFIUS filing could be triggered by foreign investors only if the product becomes ITAR/600-series critical technology (E07-F27). Needs export-control and immigration counsel before the first government conversation.

dual_use_potential.explanation: Civil buyers exist - private-5G/CBRS operators, telecom interference-hunting teams, airports and ports (GPS interference), event venues, regulators - and the shared-band policy push (NTIA Advanced DSS demonstration, NIST CBRS SEA program) keeps monitoring salient. But the civil market is thin and price-sensitive, CBRS interference is handled by SAS administrators and government measurement campaigns, premium vendors already serve regulators and telcos, and Aurora Insight is a documented failure of a standalone spectrum-data business. Medium, trending low for venture purposes.

defensibility.explanation: TDOA/AoA algorithms are published (R&S white paper, ION 2026 paper) and hardware is commodity, so code is not defensible. Per-site calibration data and a footprint of installed node networks would compound slowly; the JSIR/SFAF workflow client is copyable by DISA's contractors or the EWPMT-X integrator; government relationships (a CRADA, a DISA sponsor) would be the only real moat and are government-controlled. No network effects.

why_now: (1) Commodity coherent SDRs (KrakenSDR ~EUR 1,063) and GPSDO timing make sub-$2k geolocation nodes possible and peer-reviewed 2026 work shows jammer localization on low-cost arrays; (2) shared-spectrum policy (National Spectrum Strategy Advanced DSS demonstration at 3.1-3.45 GHz, NIST CBRS SEA measurements, GAO-26-107873) raises the salience of interference monitoring; (3) the Army proved in 2026 that cheap distributed spectrum sensors can be bought at production scale (REWSI) and that TAK is the tactical host (EWPMT-X), so an offline TAK-native client has a plausible home; (4) DISA is modernizing the enterprise stack (EMBM-J) and its SOSC support period runs to Sept 2026, a natural re-plan point. Counter: each of these has already pulled in a funded vendor or is being done in-house by government labs.
killer_risk: There is no buyer with signature authority and a budget for this scope: installation and range spectrum managers are compliance/records staff who buy handhelds, the persistent base/range sensing money went to Hidden Level (OTA), tactical EMI detection went to 3dB Labs/REWSI vendors, the ticket and assignment workflow is owned by DISA DSO (JSIRO, Spectrum XXI, EMBM-J recompete) which can add offline modes through its own contractors, and the civil market is thin and already served by R&S/CRFS/Keysight at the top and Distributed Spectrum/Wavelet Lab/KrakenSDR at the bottom - so the best case is a licensed feature or a small SaaS, not a company.

allied_extension: Only marginally. Allied regulators and militaries are the home market of Rohde & Schwarz (Germany) and CRFS (UK), so a German founder's network helps less than usual; NATO spectrum management uses its own tools and national JSIR equivalents, and civil CBRS-style sharing is U.S.-specific (Europe uses different sharing regimes). An offline TAK-native spectrum client could interest TAK-using allies (UK, Australia under the AUKUS ITAR exemption) but that is a feature sale, not a market. Allied extension does not change the verdict.
